title: What is GEO (generative engine optimisation)? A plain guide
description: GEO, or generative engine optimisation, is how a business gets named in AI answers from ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. What it is, what works, what it cannot do.
h1: What is GEO (generative engine optimisation)? A plain guide
lede: GEO, or generative engine optimisation, is how a business gets named in AI answers from ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. What it is, what works, what it cannot do.
answer: GEO, short for generative engine optimisation, is the work of making a business easy for AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews to find, understand and name in their answers. It builds on SEO (search engine optimisation); it does not replace it.

sections.html:
When you search Google the classic way, you get a list of links and you choose. When you ask an AI tool the same question, it writes one answer and often names a few businesses inside it. GEO is the work of being one of the businesses it names, and of being described correctly when it does.

Most of that work is ordinary and checkable: clear pages, accurate facts, proof behind your claims, and trustworthy sites that say the same thing about you.

The AI answer can end the search. A buyer who asks "who is the best provider of X?" may act on the shortlist in the answer without ever opening a results page. If your business is not in that shortlist, you will not see a lost click in your analytics, because the visit never started.

No, and it is not a replacement. SEO helps your pages rank and get found. GEO helps the AI tools that read those pages name you and describe you accurately. AI tools mostly work from pages they can already reach, so a site with weak SEO foundations is a weak starting point for GEO. Do SEO first and add GEO on top. The comparison of AEO, GEO and SEO shows where the three differ.

The same three letters mean other things, and AI tools do not always pick the one you intended. We tested this. On 7 October 2026 we asked ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews 30 questions each, once, and read every answer. Seven of the questions depended on the tool understanding "GEO", "AEO" or "SEO for ChatGPT" as this discipline.

  • ChatGPT answered about something else on six of the seven. It treated GEO as local or geographic SEO, or as mapping and space agencies, and answered "What is AEO?" with "Authorized Economic Operator", a customs programme.
  • Gemini gave both meanings on three of them, asked which meaning was intended once, and once explained GEO as geostationary orbit.
  • Google AI Overviews read all seven as this discipline.
  • On a related question that spelled out "generative engine optimization" in full, ChatGPT read the term correctly.

This is one test on one day. Answers vary from run to run. The lesson is practical all the same: spell the term out in titles, headings and the first sentence of any page that you want an AI tool to read this way.

1. Let the tools in. Google says a page needs to be indexed and eligible to show a snippet in normal Search, with "no additional requirements" for AI Overviews and AI Mode. For ChatGPT, OpenAI says to allow its search crawler, OAI-SearchBot, in your robots.txt file. It lists this separately from GPTBot, which relates to training.
  2. Answer the question first. Put the plain answer in the first two sentences, then explain.
  3. Spell out acronyms the first time you use them, so the tool can tell which meaning you intend.
  4. Show your evidence. Use real numbers with a date and a source, a named author with credentials, and links to primary sources.
  5. Be described the same way elsewhere. AI tools check what other sources say about you. Matching profiles, directory listings, reviews and press coverage reinforce the facts on your own site.
  6. Keep pages current. Show when each page was published and last updated.

You do not need a special file or special markup for Google's AI features. Google states that no special schema.org structured data is needed for them. Structured data is still good practice for search in general.

It cannot guarantee that an AI tool will mention you. The tools decide what to name, and they change how they decide without notice. Google itself says indexing and serving "isn't guaranteed" even when every requirement is met. Be wary of anyone who sells guaranteed AI citations. The honest promise is the work and the measurement.

Pick the 20 to 30 questions your buyers really ask. Ask each one on the same AI tools on a regular schedule. Record three things: whether your business is named, whether your website or profile is cited as a source, and whether the description is correct. Repeat monthly and compare against your first run. That first run is your baseline.

faqs.a: Generative engine optimisation. It is sometimes called AI search optimisation, and "GEO" is also used for geographic or local SEO and for other unrelated terms, so spell it out when it matters.

faqs.q: Is GEO the same as AEO?
faqs.a: They overlap heavily, and many writers use them as synonyms. AEO (answer engine optimisation) is the older term, focused on being the direct answer. GEO is usually used for being named inside AI-written answers. See AEO vs GEO vs SEO.

h1: How AI engines choose which brands to cite
lede: Generative engines cite brands they can retrieve, understand and trust. There is no paid slot. Here is the honest picture of how that choice is made.
answer: AI engines cite brands they can retrieve, parse and corroborate. They do not sell a placement inside the answer. The work is to become the clearest, most evidenced source on the prompts buyers already ask.

sections.html:
There is no public auction for “being named” in ChatGPT or Claude. Each engine retrieves sources, compresses them, and prefers pages it can parse and corroborate.

The details differ:

  • ChatGPT (and browsing / search modes) pulls from the live web and licensed data. Clear entities, original explanations and consistent brand facts help it name you without inventing a competitor.
  • Perplexity shows sources more explicitly. Domain-level citation patterns matter; a thin marketing page loses to a specific, dated explainer.
  • Google AI Overviews sit on Search. Entity understanding, structured data and classic crawl health still weigh heavily.
  • Gemini overlaps Google’s index and Workspace context. Inconsistent NAP, schema or product names confuse it.
  • Claude is often used for due diligence. It leans on sources that read like evidence, not slogans.

We will not publish a fake “citation rate by engine.” Refresh cycles, retrieval sets and safety filters change. What we can say: engines prefer pages that answer the question immediately, mark up Q&A, declare an author or organization, and match facts found elsewhere.

sections.html: They write 2,000 words that never answer the H1. They block GPTBot or PerplexityBot in robots.txt. They ship Organization schema with no logo, no sameAs, and three different legal names. They invent statistics the engine can contradict.

Optimizer360.ai runs the same buyer prompts across all five engines and records mentions, citations and framing. You can reproduce every finding by asking the engine yourself. That is the only honest scoreboard.

lede: How to get your business found in ChatGPT search: let OpenAI's search crawler in, be clear and consistent across the web, and check what ChatGPT says.
answer: To be found in ChatGPT, let OpenAI's search crawler reach your site, make your pages clear and consistent with what other sources say about you, and then ask ChatGPT what it says. There is no special trick. ChatGPT mostly answers from the web pages it can find, so the basics of SEO (search engine optimisation) still carry the weight.

sections.html: People use the phrase for two different things. One is getting your business named and linked in ChatGPT's answers. The other is using ChatGPT to write content that ranks on Google. This article is about the first. The two are easy to mix up: when we asked ChatGPT "How do I do SEO for ChatGPT?" on 7 October 2026, as one of 30 buyer questions we put to three AI tools, it answered about ranking ChatGPT-written content in Google. It is one test on one day, and answers vary, so spell out what you mean when you write about this.

ChatGPT can search the web when a question needs current information, and its answers may include links to the sources it used. OpenAI's help page also says that ChatGPT search sometimes partners with other search providers, and that it rewrites a question into one or more targeted queries to send to them. It adds that results and citations can be incomplete, outdated or incorrect.

What this means for you: ChatGPT's answer depends on what its search can retrieve, from your site and from other pages about you. If your own page is hard to find, thin or out of date, or if other pages say something different, that is what ChatGPT has to work with.

1. Let the right crawler in. OpenAI lists three crawlers separately. OAI-SearchBot is the one that surfaces sites in ChatGPT's search features, and OpenAI says a site that opts out will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, though it can still appear as a navigational link. GPTBot relates to training. ChatGPT-User handles actions a person asks for in ChatGPT. You can allow OAI-SearchBot without allowing GPTBot, and OpenAI says it can take around 24 hours for a robots.txt change to take effect.
  2. Answer the question first. Put the plain answer in the first two sentences of the page, then explain.
  3. Say the same thing everywhere. Keep your name, description, address and services identical on your site, your profiles, directories and reviews. When a search turns up different versions, ChatGPT has no way to tell which is right.
  4. Make facts easy to find. Put prices, locations, dates and claims on clear, dated pages, and link to your sources.
  5. Earn mentions on other sites. Profiles, reviews, roundups and press give a search more than one place to find you. Appearing is the publishers' decision, so plan for effort, not a guarantee.
  6. Keep pages current. An old price or a closed branch on an indexed page can end up in an answer.

You do not need a special file or special markup for this. For Google's own AI features, Google says no extra requirements or special schema are needed, and the same advice (clear, current pages that can be crawled) applies here.

• Promises of guaranteed placement. No one controls what ChatGPT names, so no one can promise an organic mention. Paid advertising, where a platform offers it, is a separate matter that this article does not cover.
  • Blocking the search crawler and expecting to appear. If OAI-SearchBot is blocked, ChatGPT search will not show the site.
  • Invented statistics and fake reviews. They are easy to check and they damage trust.

Write down the 20 to 30 questions your customers ask. Ask each in ChatGPT, on a schedule, and save the answer with its date and the sources it cites. Note three things: whether your business is named, whether your own site is cited, and whether what it says is correct. If it is wrong, find the page it came from. That page, and not ChatGPT, is what you fix. Then ask the same question again. What an AI visibility audit includes describes the full method.

title: Is SEO dead now with AI? What the data says
description: AI answers have changed how people click, but SEO is not dead. What Pew, Ahrefs, Seer Interactive and Google's own guidance show, and what to do about it.
keywords: is seo dead now with ai
h1: Is SEO dead now with AI? What the data says
lede: AI answers have changed how people click, but SEO is not dead. What Pew, Ahrefs, Seer Interactive and Google's own guidance show, and what to do about it.
answer: No. AI search has changed where people get answers and how often they click, but the pages AI tools draw on still depend on the same foundations: content worth reading, pages that can be reached and understood, and sources that agree with each other. SEO (search engine optimisation) is still the base. What is new is that being named inside an AI answer is a separate result that you now have to check.

sections.html:
More people now read a written answer before they see a list of links, and several studies show fewer clicks when that answer appears. The studies measure different things, so we set them side by side with their dates.

  • Pew Research Center (published 22 July 2025). It followed the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025. When a Google search showed an AI summary, users clicked a traditional result link in 8% of visits. Without a summary they did so in 15%. Only 1% of visits to pages with a summary involved a click on a link inside the summary. About 18% of the searches in the sample produced an AI summary.
  • Ahrefs (published 4 February 2026). It compared 300,000 keywords, half with an AI Overview and half without. For keywords that showed an AI Overview, the average click-through rate (the share of impressions that become clicks) of the top-ranking page was 0.016 in December 2025, against 0.073 in December 2023. Ahrefs puts that 58% below what it forecast without AI Overviews. It describes this as a correlation, and notes that click-through rates also fell on keywords with no AI Overview.
  • Agarwal and Sen, a working paper on SSRN (posted 3 April 2026). Participants were randomly given Google with or without AI Overviews. According to the paper's abstract, where an AI Overview appeared, outbound organic clicks fell by about 39.8% and zero-click searches rose by about 34.5%. Sponsored clicks were not affected, and people who did click through engaged with sites in the same way.
  • Seer Interactive (published 24 April 2026). It tracked 53 brands and about 5.5 million queries. On queries where Google showed an AI Overview, the organic click-through rate fell from 3.19% in January 2025 to 1.31% in December 2025, then rose to 2.36% in February 2026. On queries without an AI Overview it went from 2.75% to 3.16% to 3.82%. The authors describe the findings as directional, and say the early-2026 rise covers only two months and may not hold.
  • Google (its 2026 guide for marketers). Google says total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been "relatively stable year-over-year", and that clicks from AI Overviews are higher quality, with visitors more likely to spend time on the site. This is Google's own data, and it is not independent.

These do not cancel out. They use different samples, periods and methods. The fair reading is that where an AI answer appears, clicks to websites are lower in the experiment and in the observational data. One large data set shows the drop easing in early 2026, and Google disputes the overall picture. Nobody outside Google can see all of it.

Google's own guidance is that there are no additional requirements to appear in its AI Overviews or AI Mode, and that no special schema.org structured data is needed. A page has to be indexed and eligible to show a snippet in normal Search, and Google adds that appearing is never guaranteed. Its 2026 guide says SEO remains important whether you want to show up in traditional results or inside AI Overviews and AI Mode.

So the basics still carry the weight: pages search engines can crawl, content that answers real questions with something of its own, and a site that loads well and is easy to read.

A page can rank and still not be what an AI tool uses. The tool writes one answer from the sources it can retrieve and trust, and then decides what to name.

We saw a small version of this on 7 October 2026, when we asked ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews 30 buyer questions. Nine of them were explainers, such as what GEO (generative engine optimisation) is, and whether SEO is dead. In 24 of the 27 answers to those nine questions, the tools named no company at all. They answered from general sources. Being one of the sources an AI tool reaches for is not the same as ranking, and you can only find out by asking the tool.

It is one test on one day, and answers vary from run to run.
sections.h2: Where SEO alone stops being enough

sections.html:
Keep your SEO and add three checks.

  1. Do the SEO basics. Make pages crawlable, keep them fast, and write for the reader. This is also what Google says to do for AI Overviews.
  2. Answer first. Put the plain answer in the first two sentences of a page, spell out acronyms the first time you use them, and show the evidence behind your claims with a date and a source.
  3. Ask the AI tools yourself. Take the 20 to 30 questions your buyers ask. Ask each on ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews on a schedule. Record whether your business is named, whether your website is cited, and whether the description is right. Compare against your first run.

What an AI visibility audit includes explains this method in full. You can also read what GEO is and how AEO, GEO and SEO differ.

No one can promise that SEO will or will not recover its clicks. If your own search data showed that the questions you rely on had stopped sending visitors and no AI tool named you, that would be a real warning. The way to see it is to measure both: your search traffic, and what the AI tools say. That is a plan you can follow whatever the studies end up showing.

title: llms.txt and robots.txt for AI crawlers
description: How to allow GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended in robots.txt, and what an honest llms.txt should contain. No ranking promises.

h1: llms.txt and robots.txt for AI crawlers
lede: How to allow GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended in robots.txt, and what an honest llms.txt should contain. No ranking promises.
answer: robots.txt decides whether AI crawlers may fetch your pages. llms.txt is an optional Markdown map of the site. Neither file buys a citation; both remove avoidable reasons you are invisible.

sections.html: Two small text files do a lot of GEO damage when they are wrong.

Search and AI crawlers honour robots.txt. If you Disallow: / for GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot or Google-Extended, those systems are being told not to fetch you. That is a choice — sometimes correct for staging — and a common production accident.

A GEO-friendly policy typically:

  • Allows / for * except /admin and /api
  • Explicitly allows the major AI user agents
  • Points at your sitemap

Optimizer360.ai’s public robots policy is generated from a template that names GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, Bingbot, Applebot-Extended and others.

Confirm current official agent names in each vendor’s documentation before you copy a list from a blog.

llms.txt is a proposed convention: a Markdown file at /llms.txt that tells language models what the site is, which pages matter, and where the longer extract lives (/llms-full.txt). It is not an official Google ranking factor. It is a courtesy map.

A useful llms.txt is short, factual, and updated when you publish. It should not invent metrics. Ours lists who we are, the engines we cover, key URLs, and published articles.
Some sites add /ai.txt as a human-readable crawl policy that points at llms.txt, the sitemap and a contact address. It complements robots.txt; it does not replace it.
Do not stuff llms.txt with keyword lists. Do not claim citation rates. Do not allow bots on staging and then forget to allow them in production — or the reverse.

• llmstxt.org defines the proposed /llms.txt format. Treat it as a discovery convention, not a guaranteed citation lever. https://llmstxt.org/
  • OpenAI publishes the GPTBot / OAI-SearchBot documentation. Use the official user-agent names in robots.txt. https://platform.openai.com/docs/bots

faqs.q: Is llms.txt required for GEO?
faqs.a: No. Crawl access, clear pages and trustworthy sources matter more. llms.txt is a useful extra.

faqs.q: Should we block AI trainers but allow search bots?
faqs.a: That is a policy choice. Be explicit. Blocking all AI agents will also limit answer-engine retrieval.

title: Product data and AI shopping: what engines read
description: When shoppers ask AI what to buy, the answer rests on your product data. Here’s what Google and OpenAI say merchants should share, plus a simple checklist.
h1: Product data and AI shopping: what engines read
lede: When shoppers ask AI what to buy, the answer rests on your product data. Here’s what Google and OpenAI say merchants should share, plus a simple checklist.
answer: Picture a shopper asking AI what to buy. The answer depends on what the engine can read about your products: price, stock, descriptions and images. Google and OpenAI both let merchants hand that data over directly. The rule that matters most is a simple one: keep it accurate, current and the same everywhere.

sections.html:
Picture a shopper typing a question into an AI engine: what should I buy in your category? The answer names a product. Sometimes it quotes a price. Sometimes it even says whether the item is in stock.

So where did that come from? Increasingly, it didn’t come from your advertising. It came from your product data, and most businesses have never thought of it as a shop window.

Good news first: both Google and OpenAI let merchants share product data with them directly.

  • Google. Its documentation says structured data “can help Google understand your page better,” and that merchants can “tell Google directly which products you want to show on Google” by uploading a feed to Google Merchant Center. Participation in Merchant Center is required to appear in the Google Shopping tab.
  • OpenAI. Its commerce documentation says product feeds help ChatGPT “present accurate product information in shopping experiences.” Merchants send a structured feed with required fields for every record, and OpenAI says it is “generally recommended to provide the entire feed once a day.”

A quick, honest note on availability. OpenAI says onboarding product feeds in ChatGPT is currently open to approved partners, and shopping features can vary by country and device. So check what applies in your market before you plan around it.

Strip away the detail and both platforms are really asking for the same three things.

  • Accurate. Price and availability are what shoppers act on, so they have to be right. A mismatch costs you trust fast.
  • Current. Google says it does not guarantee how long changes on your site take to be processed, and OpenAI generally recommends refreshing the full feed once a day. Old data is wrong data, even if it was right last week.
  • Consistent. Google advises making sure your structured data matches the visible text on the page. The same principle applies across your site, your feed and your marketplace listings. When an engine sees three versions of the truth, it has no way to know which one to trust.
sections.h2: What this means in plain English

sections.html:
These are the problems we look for first. You might recognise a few.

  • An old price still showing on one channel, long after the sale ended
  • A discontinued variant that’s still listed as available
  • The same product named three different ways
  • A one-line description that tells a shopper nothing useful
  • Missing or poor-quality images
sections.h2: Where product data usually goes wrong

sections.html:
Most of these errors are invisible from the inside. Your team sees the right price on your own site, while an engine quietly quotes the old one from somewhere else.

That is what our AI visibility audit is built to surface. We run the questions your shoppers actually ask across the AI engines, and record what each one says about your products, which competitors are named instead, and which sources the answer relied on. You get a dated baseline you can verify by asking the same questions yourself. See how the engines are covered.

1. Pick one source of truth for every product, and update that first.
  2. Make everything agree. Website, feed and marketplace listings should tell the same story.
  3. Add structured data that matches what’s visible on the page.
  4. Use a feed where a platform offers one, and refresh it on a schedule.
  5. Ask the engines about your products, and read what they say. Wrong answers show you where to look.

A clean feed doesn’t guarantee a recommendation. The engines decide. What you control is whether they have accurate, current, consistent facts to work with, so that a wrong answer is never your fault. We explain how the engines weigh sources in how AI engines choose which brands to cite.

We start by asking the engines what they say about your products today. Then we trace each error back to the source behind it and work alongside your team to fix it there. Every finding is something you can check yourself by asking the engine.

In practice, an engagement follows four steps:

  • Baseline. A recorded picture of how the engines describe your products today, so progress is measured against the truth rather than memory.

Google says trust is the most important part of quality, and gives extra weight to topics that affect health and money. The brands that win are the ones whose credentials are easy to find, easy to read and easy to verify.

sections.html:
“Which hospital can I trust for my mother’s surgery?”

“Is this bank safe for my family’s savings?”

“Which business school is worth the fees?”

Nobody asks these lightly. And more and more, people ask them to an AI engine first, then to a friend, and only then to you.

Google is open about this. Its guidance on helpful content says that, of the qualities it looks for, “trust is most important.” It also gives “even more weight to content that aligns with strong E-E-A-T for topics that could significantly impact the health, financial stability, or safety of people.”

E-E-A-T stands for experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness. Google also notes that E-E-A-T is not itself a specific ranking factor. It is a way of describing what its systems try to reward.

One honest caveat. That is Google’s guidance for Google Search. We have not found comparable published guidance from other engines, so we will not claim the others work the same way. What we do know is that a worried buyer wants the same thing from any source: proof.

Google suggests three simple questions about any page. They work well as a trust checklist.

  • Who? Google asks whether it is “self-evident to your visitors who authored your content,” and whether pages carry a byline where one might be expected. A health article signed by a named doctor says more than one signed by “admin.”
  • How? Google says “it’s helpful to readers to know how a piece of content was produced.” Who reviewed it, and on what basis?
  • Why? Google calls this “perhaps the most important question,” and the right answer is content created “primarily to help people.”

It also asks whether the content offers “original information, reporting, research, or analysis.” A page that repeats what every competitor says gives an engine no reason to prefer you.

Some trust-led brands have real credentials: qualified specialists, proper licences, a long record. If those credentials live only in a brochure, a PDF or an image, an engine may not read them. The brand is then credible in person and quiet in the answer.

1. List the questions a nervous buyer asks. Use their words, not your marketing words.
  2. Answer each one on its own page, in the opening lines, signed by a named person.
  3. Put credentials in text. Google’s guidance says to make sure “important content is available in textual form.”
  4. Say only what you can back. Rules on claims in health and finance vary by country, so involve your compliance team.
  5. Check that outside sources agree with you. Directories, profiles and listings should tell the same story as your site.
  6. Ask the engines the same trust questions your buyers ask, and read what they say.

An engine can mention you prominently and still give the wrong founding year, a discontinued product, last year’s results or a namesake company’s reviews. Visibility without accuracy can cost more than absence, because the buyer believes what they read.

• Stale pages. An old press release or a third-party profile is easier to retrieve than your current page, so the engine quotes a figure that was true two years ago.
  • Entity confusion. Two companies share a name, or a group runs several businesses, and the engine merges them into one description.
  • Missing records. When no retrievable page states a fact clearly, an engine may fill the gap with something that merely sounds right.
  • Low-quality or hostile sources. A single forum thread or complaint page becomes the most quotable thing written about you.

Run the questions a buyer, investor or journalist would actually ask, across every major engine, and save each answer with its date and its cited sources. Then grade each answer line by line against a fact sheet your own team has signed off. Note the source behind every error. That source, not the engine, is what you fix.

1. Publish the correct fact where it can be retrieved. A clear, dated page that answers the question in its opening lines.
  2. Make your entity unambiguous. Google’s documentation says Organization structured data can help it understand an organisation’s details and distinguish it from others. Consistent names, logo, address and sameAs links to your official profiles all support this.
  3. Deal with the stale source. Update or retire it where you control it. Where you don’t, request a correction with evidence, not a complaint.
  4. Strengthen corroboration. The correct version should appear in more than one credible place, not only on your own site.
  5. Re-measure. Run the same prompts again and record whether the answer changed, and which source the engine now cites.

Don’t try to bury legitimate coverage or flood the web with thin pages. Engines look for corroboration, and manufactured volume tends to read as noise. Suppression attempts can also become the story themselves. And don’t expect an overnight fix: each engine refreshes its sources on its own schedule.

h1: Mentioned vs Cited in AI Answers: The 4 States Your Brand Can Be In
lede: AI engines often name your brand without linking it, or link it without naming it. See the 4 states and how to fix each.
answer: A mention is when an AI engine names your brand in its answer. A citation is when it links your page as a source. They rarely happen together: in a June 2026 Semrush study of 3,981 domain appearances, only 13.2% had both. Track each one separately, by engine, or your AI visibility numbers will mislead you.

sections.html:
1. A mention names your brand in the text of an answer. A citation links one of your pages as a source. Either can happen without the other.
  2. In one 2026 study, 61.7% of domain appearances were citations with no mention, 25.1% were mentions with no citation, and 13.2% were both.
  3. ChatGPT cited sources in 87% of appearances and mentioned brands in 20.7%. Gemini did the reverse: 83.7% mentions, 21.4% citations.
  4. Comparison queries drew about 2.4 times the brand mentions of informational queries. Informational queries drew the most citations.
  5. Mentions come from what the model and the wider web say about you. Citations come from pages the engine retrieves and credits.
  6. AI referrals are still a small share of site visits, 0.32% to 1.08% in two studies. Measure mentions and citations for what they do, not only for clicks.
  7. Run your own tally: 20 prompts, 5 runs each, 2 engines, rechecked at 30 and 90 days.

A mention is an AI engine naming your brand in the text of its answer. A citation is a source the engine links to or names as the basis for its answer. A mention gives you credit with the reader. A citation gives the reader a page to check. Either can happen without the other.
sections.h2: What is the difference between a mention and a citation in AI answers?

sections.html:
Because the two come from different steps. A mention comes from the model linking your brand to a category, either from its training data or from text it read while answering. A citation needs two retrieval steps: the engine fetches a page, then credits it as a source. A brand can clear the first and fail the second.

Adobe's brand visibility documentation draws the line this way: “A mention names your brand in the text; a citation links your page as a source.” It adds that a mention can come from training data with no retrieval step, while a citation comes from retrieval.

The engines' own documentation shows the second step is not automatic.

  • Perplexity says each answer includes “numbered citations linking to the original sources”.
  • OpenAI's web search tool returns inline citations for URLs found in search results. Its documentation separates the two ideas: the sources field lists the URLs the model consulted, and “the number of sources is often greater than the number of citations.”
  • Google describes AI Mode as giving a response “with links to supporting websites”, and says pages must be eligible to be shown as a supporting link.

Ahrefs measured the gap on the page side. Across 1.4 million ChatGPT prompts, only about half (49.98%) of the URLs ChatGPT retrieved were cited in the answer (Ahrefs, April 2026). So a page can be consulted and never cited, and a brand can be mentioned with no page behind it. In a University of Toronto preprint, Chen and Koudas found that 46% of ChatGPT's mentions of a brand the question did not name had no cited page that named it.

sections.html:
Get your brand named consistently by sources other than your own site. Engines connect a brand to a category from the wider web, so the evidence has to exist outside your pages. This is our working method, not a measured recipe.

  • Use one name. Write your brand, products and category the same way on your site, profiles and press mentions.
  • Earn independent coverage. News, industry publications and analyst pieces that describe what you do in a sentence an engine can lift.
  • Be present where buyers compare. Review sites, directories and community threads such as Reddit, where real customers describe you in their own words.
  • Get into “best X” lists honestly. Comparison questions draw the most mentions, so list pages that include you matter. Earn the place with accurate facts. Do not pay for placement and call it coverage.
  • Fix wrong facts first. A mention with an error does harm. See when AI gets your brand wrong.
sections.h2: How do I get my brand mentioned in AI answers?

sections.html:
Make each section of the page answer one question on its own, so the engine can lift it and credit it. The KDD 2024 generative engine optimization paper found that adding quotations, statistics and citations to content raised visibility in generative answers by up to 40%, while keyword stuffing fell below baseline.

  • Answer first. Open every section with a 30 to 60 word answer that makes sense when quoted alone.
  • Use statistics with full sources. Name the study, the date and the sample.
  • Put the main content in the HTML. If the answer loads only through a script, a crawler may not see it.
  • Let AI crawlers in. Check robots rules and firewalls for the crawlers of the engines you care about.
  • Add structured data. Organization, Article and FAQ markup state plainly who you are and what the page says.
  • Say who you are next to the fact. This is the fix for state 3, shown next.

So do not judge mentions and citations by clicks alone. A mention puts your name in front of a buyer who may search for you later, and that never shows up as an AI referral. Track both measures as visibility, and track visits as a separate result.

In part. Google's generative AI performance report shows impressions for links to your site in AI Overviews and AI Mode, by page, country, date and device. Its documentation describes link impressions, not brand mentions in the answer text. Bing Webmaster Tools reports how often your pages are cited and your share of citations (June 2026).

So the tools show where your pages appeared as links. They do not show whether the answer named your brand. For that, you need the tally.

sections.html:
Yes. The IAB's Measuring Visibility in the AI Era (August 2026) lists mention rate and citation rate as separate measures under “presence”. It defines mention rate as how often a brand appears in AI responses across a defined query set, and citation rate as how often it is cited as a source.

The IAB also says “single-response measurement is not measurement”, asks for results as a range, and separates directional data, which shows trends, from decision-grade data, which can support budget decisions. It leaves specific variability thresholds as an open question.
sections.h2: Is there a standard for measuring mentions and citations?

sections.html:
Run a fixed tally: 20 buyer prompts, asked 5 times each, in 2 engines, which gives 200 runs. Record each run in the sheet and recheck at 30 and 90 days. That is a set we use as a working method, not a standard. Increase the numbers if your category is crowded.

  1. Write 20 prompts in the words buyers use, with a mix of comparison, how-to and informational questions.
  2. Ask each prompt 5 times in each engine. Answers change between runs.
  3. Record for every run: whether your brand was mentioned, whether one of your pages was cited, which other brands were mentioned, and which URLs were cited.
  4. Log runs that returned no answer separately. Do not count them as “not mentioned”.
  5. Save the answer text and compare exact cited URLs, not only domains.
  6. Report each result as a share of runs, per engine, and as a range. A single yes or no hides the spread.
  7. Repeat at 30 and 90 days, with the same prompts.

Why will a tracking tool and the ChatGPT app show different results? Tools usually query engines through an API, and the authors of the Toronto preprint warn that API models need not behave like the consumer app. Prompt wording, country and the time of the run also change the answer. Compare like with like, and note which one you used.
sections.h2: How do I check mentions and citations myself?

The Optimizer360.ai platform keeps the two apart. Visibility score is the share of tracked questions where your brand appears in the answer. There is another pattern worth watching: brands that are both mentioned and cited may have a stronger chance of appearing again across repeated answers than brands that are only mentioned or only cited. However, this should be treated as an observed association, not a guarantee of repeat visibility. Citation sources can also change over time.

A domain cited today may not be cited in the next month's results, even when the prompt remains the same. This is why AI visibility should be measured across multiple runs and reviewed regularly, rather than judged from a single answer.

faqs.a: A ghost citation is when an AI engine cites your page as a source but does not mention your brand in the answer text. Semrush uses the term. In its June 2026 study of 3,981 domain appearances, 61.7% were ghost citations. The page did the work, and the credit went elsewhere or nowhere.

faqs.q: Which AI engine mentions brands most?
faqs.a: In the Semrush study, Gemini mentioned the brand in 83.7% of appearances, the highest of the four engines. Google AI Mode mentioned brands at nearly twice ChatGPT's rate. ChatGPT mentioned the brand in 20.7% of appearances but cited sources in 87%. Results vary by prompt, so test the engines your buyers use.

faqs.q: How do I get mentioned, not just cited?
faqs.a: Get your brand named consistently by sources outside your own site: independent coverage, review sites, community threads and honest inclusion in “best X” lists. Use one brand name everywhere. Then put your name next to every fact on your own pages, so a citation carries the credit with it.

faqs.q: Do AI citations drive traffic?
faqs.a: Some, but the share is small. SE Ranking found AI platforms sent 0.32% of site traffic in January to April 2026, and a Conductor study found 1.08% in 2025. Mentions can also lead buyers to search for you later, and that does not appear as an AI referral.

faqs.q: Does Google Search Console show AI citations?
faqs.a: Partly. Google's generative AI performance report shows impressions for links to your site in AI Overviews and AI Mode, by page, country, date and device. It does not report whether an answer named your brand in its text. For mentions, you need your own tally of runs across engines.

faqs.q: Can an AI engine use my page without linking to it?
faqs.a: Yes. OpenAI's documentation says the number of sources an engine consults is often greater than the number of citations it shows. Ahrefs found only about half of the URLs ChatGPT retrieved, 49.98% across 1.4 million prompts, were cited in the answer.

faqs.q: Which matters more, being mentioned or being cited?
faqs.a: Both matter, for different reasons. A mention puts your name in the buyer's shortlist, and comparison questions draw the most mentions. A citation gives the buyer a page to check and sometimes a click. Which to chase first depends on your state, so track the two separately.

faqs.q: What is generative engine optimization?
faqs.a: Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is the work of making a brand mentioned and its pages cited in answers from AI search engines and large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. It measures mentions and citations separately, by engine, and fixes the gaps.

sections.h2: Profound vs Peec AI: which should an enterprise team choose?

sections.html:
Run both tools on the same prompts, engines, countries and dates, then compare accuracy rather than dashboards. Two weeks of daily data gives you enough runs to compare day-to-day variation.

  1. Pick 100–200 prompts that map to revenue: category, comparison, pricing and problem questions, in each priority language.
  2. Lock the scope: the same engines, countries and competitor set in both tools.
  3. Spot-check raw answers: each day, run five prompts by hand and compare with what each tool recorded.
  4. Score citation accuracy: does each tool identify the same cited URLs for the same answer?
  5. Test the workflow: ask each vendor to turn one visibility gap into a recommended fix, and time how long it takes.
  6. Price the full scope: request written quotes for your real prompt count, engines, countries and agent credits.
